summary: Defines the wire image, an abstraction of the information a protocol exposes to an on-path observer that is not a participant. The idea helps explain what happens to network functions that rely on seeing traffic when more of it is encrypted. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The wire image is the information a device on the network path can observe about a communication. It includes visible packet contents, packet timing, and the observer's location in the network.

questions: how does encryption affect network functions
what is a network protocol wire image
subtitle: A way to describe the information a nonparticipant can observe in network traffic.

tldr.problem: Encryption changes what network devices can observe, but protocols also reveal information through packet sizes, timing, and other visible behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the wire image as the packets and observation metadata available to an entity that does not participate in a communication.
tldr.outcome: The abstraction helps protocol designers decide what to expose, protect, or declare invariant so that useful network functions and future protocol changes can be considered deliberately.

facts.label: What the wire image includes
facts.value: Packets, visible content, observation time, and observer vantage point

today: RFC 8546 is an Informational document published by the IAB in April 2019. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Wire Image Describes
sections.content:
A protocol defines how its participants exchange messages. It also exposes information to devices on the path that are not participants. Information that is not protected by encryption and can be interpreted from the protocol's format or behavior forms its wire image.

The RFC introduces this abstraction to help discuss how increasing use of encryption affects network functions that rely on observing traffic. It treats the wire image as a way to reason about those effects, not as a protocol of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The wire image is what a network observer can learn from a communication. Encryption can hide some information, but other parts may remain visible.

sections.title: Packets, Timing, and Observer Position
sections.content:
The wire image includes the sequence of packets, their visible contents, the time each packet is observed, and the observer's vantage point. Packet size and the time between packets can reveal information even when message contents are encrypted.

Different observers can see different wire images of the same communication because they sit at different points in the network. Observers may also combine information across packets, protocols, and other context to infer more about an endpoint or application.
sections.plainLanguage: Observers can learn from packet sizes and timing as well as readable content. What they see depends on where they observe the traffic.

sections.title: Protecting and Engineering Visible Information
sections.content:
Encryption can hide information that forwarding devices do not need. Techniques that obscure packet timing or size can reduce other clues, but they use bandwidth or add latency and cannot hide every observable property.

End-to-end integrity protection can prevent devices on the path from changing protected bits without detection, but it does not hide those bits. Timing and packet ordering also cannot be fully protected because networks can delay, drop, or reorder packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption can hide packet contents, while integrity protection can detect changes. Neither removes all clues from packet size, timing, or delivery order.

sections.title: Protocol Invariants and Ossification
sections.content:
The RFC observes that devices on the path eventually use observable protocol information. Those devices can make later changes difficult if they rely on behavior that protocol designers did not intend to preserve. This is one way a protocol can become ossified.

Designers can declare protocol invariants: visible bits or behaviors promised to remain stable across future versions. Other visible information should be protected against accidental assumptions by devices on the path, and information not intended for those devices should be encrypted when practical.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices may come to depend on details that designers did not intend to keep. Designers can state which visible parts will remain stable and protect or encrypt other information.

sections.title: Privacy, Security, and Trust in Signals
sections.content:
The wire image can expose information relevant to end-to-end privacy and security. Protocol designers should expose only information needed by the design and consider whether observers can infer additional information from traffic.

Signals intentionally exposed for network functions may be separate from the encrypted protocol's own operation. The RFC notes that devices on the path may not be able to verify whether such signals are accurate, and communicating endpoints can change their meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: Designers should consider what observers can learn from visible traffic. A signal intended for network devices may not be independently verifiable by those devices.
